turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Good afternoon, can I have you confirm your full name and date of birth? Guadalupe Rios.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: June 17th, 1965.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Thank you, Mrs. Rios. Finally cooling off out there, huh? Thank God.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I can walk in the evenings again without melting.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: That's good to hear, actually, because we're here to talk about your diabetes. You're a 1c from last week came back at 8 .4%. In April it was 7.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: I, I figured it went up.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I have to tell you something. I stopped the glipizide.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Okay, thanks for telling me. When did you stop it and what happened?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: About two months ago, I was getting shaky and sweaty in the afternoons. One time, my sugar was 62, and I almost had to pull the car over.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: That's scary and that was the right instinct. That was the 5 milligrams once a day. Yes, the 5 in the morning.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Since I stopped it,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: no more lows. And the Metformin, you're still taking that. Yes,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: 1 ,000 milligrams twice a day, with breakfast and dinner. My stomach is fine with it now. No.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Good. What are your fasting sugars running at home?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Mostly 150 to 180 in the morning.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Are you more thirsty than usual or getting up at night to pee?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Maybe a little more thirsty.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Not up at night, no. Any numbness or tingling in your feet?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Any blurry vision and when was your last eye exam? My eyes are fine. The eye exam, um,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I think it was before COVID. I know it's been a while.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: We'll take care of that today and remind me you're allergic to sulfa. Yes,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: the bactrim. I broke out in a rash all over my body.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Got it that's still in your chart. How's the family? Good.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My husband's sugar is worse than mine. They put him on insulin last month. So now we're both checking. It's like a competition.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Well, I hope you're winning. Let me look at you. Blood pressure is 128 over 76,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: pulse 80,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: weight 186 pounds,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: about the same as April.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Let me check your feet, skin looks good, no sores or calluses. Pulses are strong in both feet and you can feel the monofilament everywhere I touched. Heart and lungs sound normal. Your other labs look good too,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: kidney function is normal, the filtration rate is 78 and there's no protein in your urine okay that's good news at least it is so to put it together your type 2 diabetes is above our goal and the glipizide was causing low sugar so we'll leave that off for good keep the metformin 1000 milligrams twice a day i'd like to add a new medicine called impagloflozin 10 milligrams once a day in the morning it doesn't usually cause lows and it also protects the heart and kidneys is it a shot no it's a pill it works by letting you You pass extra sugar in the urine, so drink plenty of water and keep that area clean. If you get any itching or a yeast infection, call us, it's treatable. If you can't eat or drink because you're sick, skip it that day.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Okay, water,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I can do.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: I'm also putting in a referral for a diabetic eye exam and keep up the evening walks, they really do help.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: We'll repeat the A1C in three months and see you then. Can you send the eye doctor info to the portal? My daughter, Mary Eisler, reads it for me.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Sure, is the portal email still LupeRio65 at example .com?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: That's the one.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Great, and the Impaglaflauzin goes to your usual pharmacy. Any questions? No, I think I've got it.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Thank you, doctor.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: You're welcome. Enjoy those walks.
